name: Push/pull/legs (PPL)

card.summary: A three-way weekly training split (pushing muscles, pulling muscles, legs); popular in lifting circles, and no cited research ranks it above other splits.
card.note: Encyclopedic sources cite no comparative research on training splits.

quick.overview:
Push/pull/legs, or PPL, is a way of dividing weekly weight training into sessions: one for pushing movements and muscles, one for pulling, and one for legs. It is one of several common split types alongside full-body, upper/lower and the bro split [1].

It is commonly discussed in lifting and looksmaxxing communities as a structure for building physique. Wikipedia's section on splits is tagged as needing a better source and cites no comparative research [1].
quick.mechanism: A split distributes weekly training volume across muscle groups and days [1]. Research summarised on Wikipedia reports that with equalized volume, training frequency did not influence strength, and for muscle growth two sessions per week produced greater effects than one [1]. How these findings apply to PPL specifically is not stated in the sources.
quick.risks: No harms specific to PPL are documented in the sources consulted. General resistance-training cautions apply, such as overtraining from excessive volume [2].

lead: Push/pull/legs (PPL) is a training split that divides weekly resistance training into three kinds of session: a push day for chest, shoulders and triceps, a pull day for back and biceps, and a leg day. People use it to build a fuller, more muscular and balanced physique, since each muscle group gets its own focused session and can be trained on a regular schedule across the week.[1]

Wikipedia defines a split as how a trainee divides weekly training volume across muscle groups and days, and lists push/pull/legs alongside full-body, upper/lower and the bro split, noting that some programs alternate splits from week to week.[1] PPL is often run as a six-day rotation, which hits each muscle group twice a week, or as a three-day version that hits each once; the six-day arrangement lines up with research on training each muscle twice weekly.[4]

Studies of splits themselves are scarce. A 2024 umbrella review of resistance-training variables found weekly frequency influenced strength gains, but not hypertrophy, with volume the main driver of muscle growth and evidence on training splits described as insufficient.[4] A 2016 meta-analysis found that training each muscle twice a week produced greater hypertrophy than once a week when volume was equated.[4]

chain: Push, pull and leg sessions spread weekly volume across muscle groups

angle.text: A split organises training volume so every major muscle gets worked and then recovers before it is trained again. Lifters use PPL to develop the shoulders, back, arms, chest and legs in proportion, which shapes the overall look of the physique.

Three or six days a week, giving each muscle once or twice weekly

paras: Wikipedia lists full body, upper/lower, push/pull/legs and the bro split as common splits, and notes that some programs alternate splits from week to week.[1] In a PPL arrangement, pushing movements (and the muscles they train) are grouped on one day, pulling on another, and leg training on a third. The structure keeps muscles with overlapping roles together, so that shoulders and triceps, for instance, are worked on the same day as chest presses.

Lifting is a core appearance practice in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities, where shoulder width, back thickness, arm size and leg development all shape how a physique reads. PPL appears in these circles as a way of structuring such training. Wikipedia's bodybuilding article says muscle growth occurs during rest for up to 48 hours after a workout, and lists a lack of splitting workouts among the causes of overtraining, which is one reason lifters divide their weeks by muscle group.[3]

Per Wikipedia's summary, more weekly sessions generally produce larger strength gains, but when total volume is equalized frequency had no influence on strength.[1][2] For muscle growth, a 2016 meta-analysis found that two sessions per week per muscle produced greater effects than one, and whether three beats two remains unresolved.[4] The 2024 umbrella review reported that frequency did not affect hypertrophy and that volume carried the evidence for muscle gain.[4] A 2017 meta-analysis found higher weekly set volumes produced greater strength gains in a graded dose-response relationship.[4] Training volume is described as one of the most critical variables.[1]

No studies found comparing push/pull/legs directly with other splits. Related research covers frequency and volume: a 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of training frequency and hypertrophy,[4] a 2017 meta-analysis of weekly set volume and strength,[4] and a 2024 umbrella review that found evidence on splits insufficient.[4]
